volumes.title: January: Cool Cream, Patience
volumes.text:
January. My aunt Maud has left me three things: the dairy at Sedge Farm, two miles out of Emberwick; a brown cow named Dumpling, who dislikes me; and a wooden churn with a handle worn pale by her hands. I am Nell Harrow. I have never made butter, and mean to keep an almanac of how I learn.

Let the cream stand a day until it smells faintly sharp, and have it cool, not cold. Churn steadily. For twenty minutes nothing happens and your arm aches. Then the sound changes from a slosh to a thump, and there are yellow grains swimming in thin buttermilk.

Pour off the buttermilk and keep it. Wash the grains in cold water, pressing with a wooden paddle, until the water runs clear. Work in a pinch of salt. I made half a pound, and ate a good deal of it standing up.

volumes.title: February: Snowed-In Shortbread
volumes.text:
February. Snow to the windowsills at Sedge Farm, and no getting to Emberwick. Dumpling the cow and I have reached an understanding: I warm my hands before milking, and she does not kick the pail.

With butter in the crock and nowhere to sell it, I made my aunt Maud's shortbread, which she wrote inside the lid of the flour bin as three numbers: one, two, three. One part sugar, two parts butter, three parts flour, by weight. Rub them together with cool fingers until the crumbs hold when squeezed. Press into a tin a finger deep, prick all over with a fork, and bake in a slow oven until pale gold at the edges, about three quarters of an hour. Cut it while warm.

It is plain as a snowfield and tastes entirely of butter. I begin to see why people care whose butter it is.

volumes.title: March: What the Churn Leaves
volumes.text:
March. Mud. Every churning at Sedge Farm leaves me a jug of buttermilk, thin and sharp, and for two months I gave it to the pig. Mrs. Pettigrew of Emberwick caught me at it. She has won the butter ribbon at the Harvest Fair twelve years running, and she looked at that jug as though I were pouring away silver.

Buttermilk scones, as she told them to me over the gate. Half a pound of flour, a teaspoon of baking soda, a pinch of salt, a walnut of butter rubbed in. Stir in buttermilk with a knife until it just holds together; it will take about a teacupful. Do not knead. Pat it out thick, cut in rounds, and bake hot for a quarter of an hour.

They rose like hats. A dairy wastes nothing, she said, and went off before I could thank her.

volumes.title: April: Grass Butter
volumes.text:
April. Dumpling the cow went out to the new grass at Sedge Farm on the ninth, and by the twelfth my butter had changed colour. Winter butter is pale as candle wax. This is yellow as a primrose, and softer, and smells of the meadow. I did nothing to deserve it. The grass did.

To honour it, a green butter. Chop a handful of chives and parsley from the garden bed, very fine, with a few leaves of mint. Beat them into a quarter pound of soft butter with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt. Roll it in a damp cloth into a log, chill it in the dairy, and cut coins from it as wanted.

A coin of it melting on a boiled egg, or on hot bread, is my whole supper tonight. I have written "April" on the cloth so I shall remember.

volumes.title: May: The Butter Print
volumes.text:
May. The best butter of the year comes now, when the Lowlands grass is tall, and everyone in Emberwick knows it. On market day I sold nine pounds from Sedge Farm before ten o'clock.

Mrs. Pettigrew's stall was beside mine. Every pat of hers carried a print, a thistle pressed in with a carved wooden stamp. Mine were bare. In my aunt Maud's dresser I have since found hers: a little cow, much worn, lying under a tree. Soak the stamp in cold water first or the butter will stick.

For supper, new potatoes, the first of the year. Scrub them, do not peel. Boil in salted water with a sprig of mint until a knife slides in, about fifteen minutes. Drain, return to the warm pan, and add a generous knob of May butter and a little chopped mint. Shake. Eat them from the pan.

volumes.title: June: A Crock in the Stream
volumes.text:
June. Heat. The cream at Sedge Farm turns before I can churn it, and what butter I make goes to oil on the dairy shelf. My aunt Maud's answer, I learned from a neighbour, was the stream. I now churn at five in the morning, pack the butter in a lidded stone crock, and stand the crock in the shallows under the alder with a flat rock on top. By noon it is firm as January.

With eggs plentiful, a weighing cake. Weigh three eggs in their shells. Take the same weight each of butter, sugar and flour. Beat butter and sugar until pale, add the eggs one at a time, and fold in the flour with a teaspoon of baking powder. Bake in two tins in a moderate oven for twenty-five minutes.

Sandwich it with jam. Dumpling watched me eat it over the gate, unimpressed.

volumes.title: July: Clear Gold
volumes.text:
July. Mrs. Pettigrew of Emberwick stopped at my stall and asked, not unkindly, how I meant to keep butter through the hot weeks. I had no answer. She told me to clarify it, and then looked as though she regretted giving away so much.

Melt a pound of butter in a heavy pan over the lowest heat. Do not stir. A white foam rises; skim it off. Milky dregs sink to the bottom. When the middle is clear as amber, pour it gently through a clean cloth into a warm jar, leaving the dregs behind.

What you have is butter with the parts that burn and spoil taken out. It keeps for weeks in the cool, and it will fry a pancake or an egg at a heat that would blacken ordinary butter. I fried mushrooms from the market in it, and wrote "clear gold" on the jar.

volumes.title: August: Brown Butter, Burnt Butter
volumes.text:
August. The Harvest Fair at Emberwick is five weeks off, and I have entered a pound of Sedge Farm butter against Mrs. Pettigrew's. I think of little else, which is how I came to burn a pan of it.

Brown butter is butter cooked a minute past melting. Put a good lump in a pale pan, so that you can see the colour. It foams, then quietens, and the specks at the bottom turn the brown of a hazelnut shell. It smells of nuts and toast. Take it off the heat at that moment and pour it out, because the pan goes on cooking.

Mine went black while I stared out of the window, composing a speech of thanks. The second lot I watched. I poured it over runner beans with a squeeze of lemon, and it was better than any speech. Attend to the pan.

volumes.title: September: The Fair
volumes.text:
September. The Harvest Fair. Twenty pounds of butter sat on the long table in the Emberwick market hall, each under a numbered cloth. The judge tasted them with a horn spoon, and spent a long time over two.

Mrs. Pettigrew took the ribbon, her thirteenth. I had a card that said Second. I had expected to mind more than I did.

She found me afterwards by the cake stall and told me what she has told nobody. Wash it once more than you think it needs, because any buttermilk left in will sour the butter within the week. Then salt it properly: a small level teaspoon of fine salt to the pound, worked through until no streaks show. Press out every bead of water. "Yours was the better cream," she said. "Mine was the better washed." Her hands, I noticed, were stiff on the spoon.

volumes.title: October: Apples and Cold Hands
volumes.text:
October. Mrs. Pettigrew's hands are too stiff now to turn a churn. I walk into Emberwick on Tuesdays and Fridays and churn for her, and she sits by and corrects me. I learn more in an hour there than in a month alone at Sedge Farm.

She says butter pastry wants what butter wants: cold, and not much handling. Half a pound of flour, a quarter pound of cold butter cut small, a pinch of salt. Rub in with the fingertips only, lifting, until it looks like crumbs. Add cold water a spoonful at a time until it gathers. Rest it somewhere cool for half an hour.

Roll it out, cut rounds, and fold each over a spoonful of sliced apple, sugar and a little cinnamon. Pinch shut, brush with milk, bake hot for twenty minutes. We ate four turnovers between us, and she allowed that they would do.

volumes.title: November: The Lean Month
volumes.text:
November. Dumpling the cow is to calve at midwinter, and I have stopped milking her so that she may rest. There will be no cream at Sedge Farm for weeks. I have six pounds of salted butter in crocks and one jar of clarified, and I count them as a miser counts.

Mrs. Pettigrew of Emberwick says that butter you cannot make must be made to go further, and showed me a spiced butter for cold evenings. Beat a quarter pound of soft butter with two spoonfuls of brown sugar, a teaspoon of cinnamon and a scrape of nutmeg until light. Keep it in a small pot.

A little goes a long way. Spread it thin on hot toast or oatcakes by the fire, and it melts into something like a pudding. I took her a pot of it. I find I have stopped counting what I give her.

volumes.title: December: The Year Turns
volumes.text:
December. Dumpling calved on the shortest day, by lantern light: a brown heifer with a white star, already cross. I have named her Crumb. There is milk in the pail again at Sedge Farm.

For the midwinter market Mrs. Pettigrew and I shared one stall in Emberwick, her thistle print and my aunt Maud's little cow side by side. We sold butter biscuits. Rub six ounces of butter into half a pound of flour, stir in four ounces of sugar, the grated rind of an orange and one egg yolk, and knead lightly to a dough. Roll, cut, press the wet stamp on each, and bake in a moderate oven until just gold, about twelve minutes.

A year ago I could not make butter. Now my hands know when the churn is about to turn. For whoever keeps this almanac next: begin with cool cream, and patience.

volumes.title: The First Wet Evening
volumes.text:
First day of rain. I am Hester Lumb, cook at the Ferry House, where the Emberwick road meets the river Ember and stops. It began at noon. By dusk Corwen the ferryman had tied up the boat and said the river was not to be argued with. One traveller is stranded already: a wool merchant, Mr. Garrick, who takes the weather personally.

So, onion soup, which wants only time. Slice four large onions thin. Cook them in butter in a heavy pot over a low fire for the better part of an hour, stirring now and then, until they are soft and brown as a saddle. Add a spoonful of flour, then a quart of stock and a bay leaf. Simmer twenty minutes.

Ladle it over toast with cheese on top. Mr. Garrick said it would do. I shall write down a soup each day until the ferry runs.

volumes.title: Leeks for Wet Travellers
volumes.text:
Second day of rain at the Ferry House. The river Ember is over the lower landing step. Three more came in off the road, dripping: Mr. Pell, a clock-mender with a case of small wheels, and two sisters, the Misses Finch, bound for market with a goose named Duchess on a ribbon. The goose has the wash-house. The rest have my kitchen fire.

Leek and potato soup is the quickest comfort I know. Wash three leeks well, for they hold grit, and slice them. Soften them in butter with the lid on. Add four potatoes cut small, cover with stock, salt it, and simmer until the potato breaks under a spoon, about twenty minutes. Mash it roughly in the pot and stir in a little milk.

Five bowls came back wiped clean with bread. Even Mr. Garrick, the wool merchant, had seconds, though he did not say so.

volumes.title: Pease and Complaints
volumes.text:
Third day of rain. The ferry has not crossed the Ember since Monday, and my four stranded guests at the Ferry House are beginning to know each other's faults. Mr. Garrick the wool merchant has explained to everyone what the delay is costing him. Mr. Pell the clock-mender has taken the kitchen clock apart on my table, to be useful.

Split pea soup. Soak a pound of dried split peas overnight. Drain them and simmer in fresh water with a chopped onion, a carrot and a sprig of thyme. Skim the froth. In an hour and a half the peas fall to a thick green porridge; thin it with hot water, salt it at the end, and stir in chopped mint.

It sticks to the ribs. Mr. Garrick complained that it was green. Tam, my pot-boy, ate three bowls and fell asleep in the settle.

volumes.title: Barley Broth and a Clock
volumes.text:
Fourth day of rain at the Ferry House, and the river Ember has taken the whole landing. Corwen the ferryman sits at the window watching his boat tug at her rope. In my kitchen the clock is back on the wall. Mr. Pell, the stranded clock-mender, has made it strike the hours, which it has not done since my mother's time.

For that he had first bowl of the barley broth. Rinse a teacup of pearl barley. Put it in the pot with two carrots, a turnip, an onion and a stick of celery, all cut small, and three pints of stock. Simmer gently for an hour, until the barley is fat and soft. Salt, pepper, and a handful of chopped parsley at the last.

It is plain, and nobody was ever sorry to see it. The clock struck six as I served. We all jumped.

volumes.title: Mushrooms, Not from the Wood
volumes.text:
Fifth day of rain. Tam, the pot-boy here at the Ferry House, came in from the wet wood with a hatful of mushrooms and a hopeful face. I thanked him and put them on the compost. I do not trust my eye with wild ones, and no soup is worth a wrong guess. The mushrooms in this pot came from the grower's trays at Emberwick market before the river rose.

Wipe a pound of them, do not wash, and slice. Cook an onion soft in butter, add the mushrooms and a pinch of thyme, and let them give up their juice and take it back again. Stir in a spoonful of flour, then a pint and a half of stock. Simmer fifteen minutes, add a cup of milk, and warm it through without boiling.

The Misses Finch pronounced it the best yet. Their goose, Duchess, got the bread crusts.

volumes.title: Dumplings When Bread Runs Out
volumes.text:
Sixth day of rain, and no bread. The baker's cart cannot reach the Ferry House, for the Emberwick road is under water at the dip, and my guests have eaten the last loaf. Mr. Garrick, the stranded wool merchant, asked what a soup was without bread. I said he would find out at six.

Dumplings. Mix four heaped spoonfuls of flour with a teaspoon of baking powder, a pinch of salt and chopped parsley. Rub in two spoonfuls of cold butter. Add just enough cold water to make a soft dough, and roll it into balls the size of a walnut with floured hands.

Drop them into any simmering broth; I used yesterday's vegetable. Put the lid on and leave it on for fifteen minutes, however curious you feel. They come up twice the size and light as pillows. Mr. Garrick counted his, and then counted Mr. Pell's.

volumes.title: Beans and a Leaking Roof
volumes.text:
Seventh day of rain. The roof of the Ferry House has begun to leak above the stairs, and Tam the pot-boy has set my second-best pan under the drip. It rings like a slow bell all night. A week now, and the river Ember still too high for the ferry. The stranded guests have stopped asking Corwen when.

White bean soup. Soak half a pound of dried white beans overnight in plenty of water. Drain, cover with fresh water, and boil them hard for ten full minutes before turning down to a simmer; dried beans must always have that hard boil. Cook until tender, an hour or more. Add a softened onion, a carrot, a bay leaf, and salt only at the end.

Crush some of the beans against the side of the pot to thicken it. It is a patient soup for people who need patience.

volumes.title: The Goose Pays Her Way
volumes.text:
Eighth day of rain, and at breakfast Mr. Garrick the wool merchant looked through the wash-house door at Duchess, the Misses Finch's white goose, and wondered aloud how many she would feed. The elder Miss Finch stood up. I have not seen a man so thoroughly looked at. Nothing more was said.

Duchess, perhaps hearing, laid an egg by noon. It was a large one, and the sisters presented it to my kitchen at the Ferry House with some ceremony.

So tonight, egg-thread broth. Bring a quart of clear, well-seasoned stock to a gentle simmer. Beat the egg in a cup with a spoonful of cold water. Stir the broth slowly in one direction and pour the egg in a thin stream; it sets at once into soft gold threads. Take it off the heat, add chopped chives, and serve directly. Mr. Garrick ate his very quietly.

volumes.title: Parsnip, Apple, Almost Nothing
volumes.text:
Ninth day of rain at the Ferry House. I took a candle down to the larder and came up with what there was: five parsnips, three wrinkled apples from the loft, one onion, and the heel of a pot of cream. The river Ember has kept the ferry tied up since the first day, and nothing has come in.

It makes a better soup than it sounds. Peel and chop the parsnips and onion and soften them in butter. Add the apples, peeled and cored, and a quart of water with a pinch of salt. Simmer until everything is tender, half an hour. Mash it smooth with a wooden spoon, or push it through a sieve if you have a willing pot-boy. Stir in the cream.

It is sweet and pale. Mr. Pell the clock-mender asked for the recipe, and wrote it on the back of a watch paper.

volumes.title: Mr. Garrick's Bread Soup
volumes.text:
Tenth day of rain, and nothing to put in a pot but water, garlic, and the dry ends of last week's loaves. I said as much aloud. It was Mr. Garrick, the wool merchant, stranded here at the Ferry House since the first evening and cross for every hour of it, who got up from the settle.

His mother made bread soup, he said. He rolled up his sleeves. Warm three sliced cloves of garlic in a little butter, slowly, without browning. Add a quart of water, a bay leaf, thyme, and salt, and simmer ten minutes. Tear in stale bread, two good handfuls, and let it swell until the soup is thick. Beat it with a spoon. A grating of hard cheese on top, if there is any.

There was a rind. He stirred the pot himself and served everyone before he sat down. Nobody mentioned it.

volumes.title: Everybody's Pot
volumes.text:
Eleventh day. The rain stopped in the night; I woke because the pan under the leak had gone quiet. But the river Ember is still brown and wide, and Corwen the ferryman says tomorrow, not today. One more supper, then, for my stranded guests at the Ferry House, and the larder bare.

So everyone turned out their bags. The Misses Finch had a twist of dried sage and six carrots meant for market. Mr. Pell the clock-mender produced an onion from his coat, unexplained. Mr. Garrick gave a paper of peppercorns he had been saving. Tam found barley at the bottom of the bin.

Into one pot: the onion softened, carrots sliced, a handful of barley, water to cover well, sage, salt. An hour's gentle simmer. Pepper ground over at the table. It was not the best soup of the eleven, but it was the one we all leaned over.

volumes.title: The Ferry Runs
volumes.text:
Twelfth day, and sun on the wet slates. Corwen took the ferry across the Ember at eight with all of them aboard: the Misses Finch and their goose Duchess, Mr. Pell with his case of wheels, and Mr. Garrick the wool merchant, who shook my hand and left his peppercorns on the dresser. The Ferry House is very quiet. The mended clock strikes into an empty kitchen.

The last recipe is the one all the others began with. Keep a stockpot. Into it go onion skins, carrot ends, parsley stalks, celery tops and any clean bones, covered with cold water and simmered very gently for two hours, then strained and kept cold. Use it within two days.

Mine is on the fire now. I have copied out the twelve soups fair and put this book above the flour bin. It will rain again. We shall be ready.

volumes.title: Four in the Morning
volumes.text:
I am Wilf Aske, fourteen, and since Monday I am apprenticed to Mrs. Marrable at the bakehouse on Oven Lane in Emberwick. She has given me this book and told me to write down each bake once I have truly learned it. She says there are a dozen worth knowing. "A baker's dozen," she added, and would not explain.

First, the plain loaf. We begin at four, in the dark. A pound and a half of strong flour, two teaspoons of salt, a teaspoon of yeast, and warm water, about three quarters of a pint. Mix, then knead for ten minutes, until the dough is smooth and springs back from a thumb.

Cover it and leave it somewhere warm until doubled. Knock it down, shape it, let it rise again in the tin, and bake hot for thirty-five minutes. A done loaf sounds hollow when you knock underneath.

volumes.title: Thirteen to the Dozen
volumes.text:
My second month at Mrs. Marrable's bakehouse on Oven Lane, and she has put me on rolls. It is the plain loaf dough, cut into pieces the weight of a hen's egg. Cup your hand over a piece and move it in small circles until it tightens into a ball with a smooth skin. My first forty looked like knuckles.

Set them on a tray, not quite touching. Let them rise until they lean on each other, brush with milk, and bake hot for fifteen minutes.

For every dozen, Mrs. Marrable has me shape a thirteenth. The dozen go to the shop. The thirteenth goes on a tin plate by the back door, and by the time I have swept the plate is empty. I asked who it was for. "The dozen is for the shop," she said. I am Wilf, her apprentice, and that is no answer.

volumes.title: Oatcakes on the Griddle
volumes.text:
Third bake in my apprentice book. Mrs. Marrable says a baker in Emberwick who cannot make an oatcake will be laughed at as far as the Northern Fells, where they eat little else.

No yeast, and no oven. Half a pound of fine oatmeal, a pinch each of salt and baking soda, and a spoonful of melted butter. Pour in hot water, a little at a time, and mix to a stiff paste. Work fast, for it sets as it cools. Roll it thin on an oatmeal-dusted board and cut rounds, then quarters.

Bake them on a hot dry griddle, three minutes a side, until the edges curl. They should snap. Mine bent, the first day, and went to the hens. I, Wilf, counted twelve of the second batch for the shop and put a thirteenth on the plate by the back door. It was gone by six.

volumes.title: Buns with Currants
volumes.text:
Wilf Aske, apprentice, fourth bake. This week Mrs. Marrable let me make the currant buns that sell out by nine every Saturday at the bakehouse on Oven Lane.

It is an enriched dough, which means it is spoiled like a favourite child. To a pound of flour, a teaspoon each of salt and yeast, add two ounces of sugar, two of soft butter, one egg, and warm milk in place of water. It is sticky and slow. Knead it anyway, and work in a handful of currants.

Shape into buns, let them rise until puffy, and bake fairly hot for fifteen minutes. Brush them at once with sugar melted in a spoonful of milk, so they shine. I asked again who takes the thirteenth from the plate by the back door. "Who is in the lane before we open?" she said. Nobody, I said. "Look harder."

volumes.title: Gingerbread, Melted and Stirred
volumes.text:
Fifth bake. Half a year at the bakehouse on Oven Lane, and Mrs. Marrable says I may be trusted with treacle.

Gingerbread is made backwards from bread: nothing is kneaded and everything is melted. Gently warm four ounces of butter with four of dark sugar and six of black treacle until it runs. Off the heat, stir in half a pound of flour sifted with two teaspoons of ground ginger and one of baking soda. Beat in an egg and a quarter pint of warm milk. It will be thin as paint. Bake it in a lined tin in a slow oven for an hour.

It is better on the third day than the first. I, Wilf, have been watching the back door, where each morning's thirteenth roll vanishes from its plate. This morning, at half past five, there was a shadow on the glass.

volumes.title: Jam Tarts and Restraint
volumes.text:
Sixth bake in the apprentice book of Wilf Aske, Oven Lane, Emberwick. Mrs. Marrable says pastry is the opposite of bread. Bread likes warm hands and hard work. Pastry likes cold hands and to be left alone.

Half a pound of plain flour, four ounces of cold butter, a pinch of salt. Rub the butter in with fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, and bring it together with very little cold water. Rest it. Roll it thin, cut rounds, and press them into the tart tin.

Now the lesson: one small teaspoon of jam in each. Jam boils up. Bake them hot for twelve minutes and let them cool before eating, for hot jam bites. The thirteenth roll we leave by the back door each morning goes, I have learned, to Mr. Lunn the lamplighter, on his way home as we begin. He touches his cap to the oven.

volumes.title: The Loaf That Fell
volumes.text:
Seventh entry, and it is a failure, written down by order of Mrs. Marrable. I, Wilf Aske, apprentice, left forty loaves rising in the warm corner of the bakehouse and went to watch the carrier's horse being shod. I came back to dough risen over the tins, slack and full of bubbles. In the oven the whole batch sank like tired hats.

The test: press a floured finger into the dough. If the dent springs back at once, wait. If it fills slowly, bake now. If it does not fill at all, you have been watching a horse.

We did not waste it. Slice and butter a fallen loaf, layer it in a dish with currants and sugar, and pour over a pint of milk beaten with two eggs. Let it soak half an hour and bake until set and brown. It sold out. I was not praised.

volumes.title: Grandmother in the Crock
volumes.text:
Eighth bake. On the cold shelf of the bakehouse on Oven Lane sits a brown crock under a cloth, and in it lives something Mrs. Marrable calls Grandmother. It is old dough. Every day she saves a fistful from the morning's batch, and next day it goes into the new dough, as it did in her mother's time.

To use it: break a piece of yesterday's dough the size of an apple into the warm water, squeeze it to a milk, then mix the plain loaf as usual, with half the yeast. Give it longer to rise. The loaf comes out with a chewier crumb, a darker crust and a faint sourness, and it keeps two days longer.

Before you shape the loaves, save a fistful back. That is the whole rule. I, Wilf, the apprentice, forgot once. Mrs. Marrable had kept a second crock, and said nothing.

volumes.title: The Harvest Plait
volumes.text:
Ninth bake. For the Harvest Fair every bakehouse in Emberwick sends a plaited loaf to the market hall, and this year Mrs. Marrable said the one from Oven Lane would be mine. I am Wilf, her apprentice. I did not sleep much.

Use the currant bun dough without the currants, a little stiffer. Divide it in three and roll each piece into a rope as long as your forearm, fatter in the middle. Pinch them together at the top. Then right over middle, left over middle, not pulling, until you reach the end. Pinch and tuck under.

Let it rise until puffy but not doubled, or the plait will blur. Brush it with beaten egg and bake fairly hot for half an hour, until deep gold. Mine leaned to the left. Mrs. Marrable carried it to the hall herself, at arm's length, as though it were a crown.

volumes.title: Scones and a Light Hand
volumes.text:
Tenth bake. Mrs. Marrable's sister is poorly on the Grey Coast, and she talks of going to her for a week. First, she says, I must learn the scone, for the Thursday customers at Oven Lane forgive a baker anything but a flat one.

Half a pound of self-raising flour, a pinch of salt, two ounces of cold butter rubbed in, an ounce of sugar. Make a well and pour in a quarter pint of milk. Mix with a knife in a few strokes, only until it holds. Pat it an inch thick with your hand; no rolling pin.

Cut straight down with a floured cutter and lift straight up. Never twist: a twisted scone rises crooked. Brush the tops with milk and bake hot for twelve minutes. I, Wilf, twisted the first six out of habit. They came out leaning, like men in a wind.

volumes.title: A Loaf Soaked in Tea
volumes.text:
Eleventh bake, for midwinter. Mrs. Marrable leaves tomorrow for her sister's on the Grey Coast, and for one week the bakehouse on Oven Lane will be in my hands. Today she taught me the tea loaf, the kindest thing in the book: it cannot be hurried and cannot easily go wrong.

The night before, put three quarters of a pound of mixed dried fruit with six ounces of brown sugar and pour over half a pint of cold tea. By morning the fruit is fat. Stir in one beaten egg and half a pound of self-raising flour with a teaspoon of mixed spice. Bake in a lined tin in a slow oven for an hour and a half.

Wrap it and keep it two days before cutting. She has left me, Wilf, the keys. She has also left the tin plate by the back door, washed, for the thirteenth roll.

volumes.title: The Thirteenth
volumes.text:
I am Wilf Aske, and for a week I have run the bakehouse on Oven Lane while Mrs. Marrable was away. Each morning I put the thirteenth roll on the plate by the back door, and this week I watched. Mr. Lunn the lamplighter came, going home cold. So did the night shelver from Emberwick Library, yawning, and the carrier's boy. They had been up so the town could sleep. The first bread is theirs.

This book holds eleven bakes and one failure, which Mrs. Marrable counts as the twelfth. The thirteenth is my own. Take the roll dough, knead in a spoonful of honey and a handful of oats, shape, brush with milk, and press the tops in more oats. Bake hot for fifteen minutes.

She came home, ate one standing, and said nothing. Next morning there was a second name on the board, small, under hers.

volumes.title: January: An Empty Shelf
volumes.text:
January. The pantry shelf at my house on Marsh Lane, Emberwick, held forty jars every winter for thirty years. This winter it holds two. My wife Marjorie made the pickles, and I, Ambrose Tull, retired schoolmaster, only ate them. I have found her receipt book and mean to work through the year with it.

One page is nearly blank. It is headed Garden Pickle, the yellow one everybody asked for, and underneath she wrote only: "You know how." I do not.

I began with something she did write down. Red cabbage: shred a firm head finely, layer it in a bowl with a good handful of salt, and leave it overnight. Next day rinse and drain it well, pack it into clean jars, and cover it with cold spiced vinegar. It is ready in a week and best eaten within two months, while it still has its crunch.

volumes.title: February: The Vinegar Itself
volumes.text:
February. My wife Marjorie's receipt book says "spiced vinegar" on every page and explains it on none. I, Ambrose Tull, taught arithmetic for forty years and expect a sum to show its working. Mrs. Abbot next door on Marsh Lane showed me.

To a quart of malt vinegar add a spoonful each of black peppercorns and mustard seed, six cloves, a few allspice berries, two bay leaves and a piece of dried ginger. Warm it gently in a covered pan until it just steams; do not boil it or the kitchen will make you weep. Leave it covered until cold, and strain it into a bottle. It keeps for months and is the start of everything.

I asked Mrs. Abbot about the Garden Pickle, the one Marjorie never wrote down. She shut her eyes. "Yellow," she said. "Bright as a daffodil. That is all I am sure of."

volumes.title: March: Beetroot and a Clue
volumes.text:
March. The last stored beetroot came up from the cellar at Marsh Lane looking like old boots. I am Ambrose Tull, a year into widowhood and three months into pickling, and I have learned not to judge by the outside.

Wash the beets without breaking the skin, or they bleed. Boil them whole until a skewer goes in easily, an hour for large ones. Cool them, rub off the skins with your thumbs, and slice. Pack the slices in jars. Warm a pint of spiced vinegar with two spoonfuls of sugar until it dissolves, let it cool, and pour it over. Ready in three days; eat within two months.

The carrier, taking a jar, said my wife Marjorie's Garden Pickle had been sweet as well as sharp. "Not sugar only. Something from the orchard in it." I have written that beside her blank page: yellow; sweet; orchard.

volumes.title: April: Rhubarb Takes Its Turn
volumes.text:
April. Nothing is ready in the garden at Marsh Lane except rhubarb, which is ready all at once. My late wife Marjorie's book has a chutney for it, with a note: "Ambrose will say it is too sharp. He will be wrong."

Cut two pounds of rhubarb short and put it in a wide pan with two chopped onions, half a pound of brown sugar, half a pint of vinegar, a spoonful of grated ginger, a handful of raisins and a teaspoon of salt. Simmer it gently, stirring often, for about an hour. It is done when a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a path that stays open a moment.

Jar it hot in clean warm jars, cover, and leave it a month to mellow. I tasted it from the spoon and thought it too sharp. I, Ambrose Tull, expect to be wrong.

volumes.title: May: Radishes in an Hour
volumes.text:
May. The radishes at Marsh Lane came up thick as a hedge, because I, Ambrose Tull, do not yet know how to sow thinly. My wife Marjorie's receipt book calls this one a quick pickle, for the impatient.

Slice a bunch of radishes thin. Warm a teacup of vinegar with a teacup of water, a spoonful of sugar and a teaspoon of salt, until they dissolve. Pour it over the radishes. In an hour the liquid is pink and the radishes crisp and sharp. Keep them cold and eat within the week.

Mrs. Abbot, my neighbour, ate half the bowl and gave me another clue to the Garden Pickle that she never wrote down. "Hers had a bite to it. The vegetables were never cooked soft. She salted them overnight in the blue bowl; I saw her do it." I have fetched the blue bowl down from the top shelf.

volumes.title: June: Yellow, but Not Hers
volumes.text:
June. The first small cucumbers, and a pickle in my wife Marjorie's book that comes out yellow. I, Ambrose Tull, thought I had found her unwritten Garden Pickle hiding under another name.

Slice four cucumbers and two onions thin. Toss them with two spoonfuls of salt and leave them for two hours; then rinse and drain well. Warm half a pint of vinegar with six ounces of sugar, a spoonful of mustard seed and a teaspoon of turmeric until the sugar dissolves. Add the vegetables, bring it just to the simmer, and jar it at once. Keep it cool and eat within two months.

I carried a jar next door to Mrs. Abbot in triumph. She tasted it. "The right colour," she said. "That is the turmeric, then. But hers had more in it, Mr. Tull. A whole garden." So: one spice found. The rest still missing.

volumes.title: July: Nasturtium Seeds, a Plan
volumes.text:
July. The nasturtiums have run over the fence at Marsh Lane and set fat green seeds, which my wife Marjorie pickled and called her capers. Pick them young. Soak them overnight in salted water, a spoonful of salt to a pint. Drain, dry on a cloth, and cover in a small jar with cold spiced vinegar. Leave them a month. They are peppery, and excellent chopped over fish from the Grey Coast.

While hunting for a small jar I, Ambrose Tull, found something better. Inside the back cover of her book she had drawn the kitchen garden, bed by bed. One bed is marked with a circled P, and in it she wrote: cauliflower, French beans, small onions, one marrow.

She never wrote out her Garden Pickle. She planted it. It is too late to sow cauliflower this year, but Mr. Oakes the grocer sells them.

volumes.title: August: The Marrow Problem
volumes.text:
August. I, Ambrose Tull, planted six marrow seeds in the garden at Marsh Lane, in case some failed. None failed. I have left marrows on every doorstep in the lane, and found two returned to mine after dark.

My wife Marjorie's book has the answer, under the heading Glut. Peel a large marrow, take out the seeds, and cut the flesh into small dice. Salt it, leave it overnight to draw the water, and drain. Simmer it with a pound of chopped onions, a pound of chopped apples, a pound of sugar, a pint of vinegar, a spoonful of ground ginger and a few peppercorns, for an hour and a half, until thick and golden.

Jar it hot and keep it six weeks before opening. I shall need one marrow more, a small one, in October, for the Garden Pickle she never wrote down. I have dozens.

volumes.title: September: Onions and Tears
volumes.text:
September. Three pounds of pickling onions from Mr. Oakes the grocer in Emberwick. Pour boiling water over them, leave a minute, and the skins slip off. You will cry regardless. Leave them overnight in a bowl with a good handful of salt; rinse and dry them next day. Pack into jars and cover with cold spiced vinegar. They want six weeks at least.

Mr. Oakes weighed the onions and eyed me over his spectacles. Every September for thirty years, he said, Mrs. Tull bought the same things: mustard powder, turmeric, ground ginger. "And she always asked had I a windfall apple or two, for the yellow pickle."

So there is the orchard. I, Ambrose Tull, went home to Marsh Lane and added it to the list beside my wife Marjorie's blank page: yellow, sweet, crisp, a whole garden, mustard, ginger, apple. It looks nearly like a recipe.

volumes.title: October: The Attempt
volumes.text:
October. Today I, Ambrose Tull, made my wife Marjorie's unwritten Garden Pickle from nine months of other people's memories.

A small cauliflower in florets, a handful of French beans, a dozen small onions and half a small marrow, all cut thumbnail-small. Salt them overnight in the blue bowl, then rinse and drain. For the sauce, mix two spoonfuls of mustard powder, one of flour, a teaspoon each of turmeric and ground ginger, and four ounces of sugar to a paste with a little vinegar. Stir in the rest of a pint of vinegar and simmer until thick. Add the vegetables and one grated windfall apple, and cook five minutes only, to keep the bite. Jar it hot.

It is yellow as a daffodil. I tasted it from the spoon in the kitchen at Marsh Lane. It is close. It is harsh, too, and something is not there.

volumes.title: November: Windfalls and Waiting
volumes.text:
November. Six jars of yellow Garden Pickle sit on the shelf at Marsh Lane, and I, Ambrose Tull, do not much like them. It was my attempt at the receipt my wife Marjorie never wrote down. I told Mrs. Abbot next door that I had failed. She asked when I made it. Three weeks ago, I said.

"Then you have not tasted it yet," she said. "Marjorie never opened hers before midwinter. Go and do something else."

So, apple chutney from the last windfalls. Two pounds of apples, peeled and chopped, a pound of onions, half a pound of sultanas, a pound of brown sugar, a pint of vinegar, a teaspoon each of ginger and salt. Simmer for an hour and a half until thick, stirring often, and jar it hot. It, too, wants a month. I am learning to shut the pantry door and walk away.

volumes.title: December: You Know How
volumes.text:
December. On midwinter eve I, Ambrose Tull, asked the neighbours of Marsh Lane to supper: bread, cheese, cold ham, and a jar of my yellow Garden Pickle, two months old. I opened it at the table. The harshness had gone out of it and the mustard had come round, as a cross child does.

Mrs. Abbot tasted it twice. "It is not Marjorie's," she said. "It is very good. Hers was never the same two years running, you know. She put in whatever the bed gave her. That is why she never wrote it down."

There are forty jars on the pantry shelf again, each labelled with what it is and the month it was made. After supper I opened my wife's book to the page that says only "You know how," and wrote my receipt beneath, with the year. The facing page I have left blank.
